newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Statistics NZ to improve timeliness of GDP data.
newsitem.headline: Statistics NZ to improve timeliness of GDP data.

text.p: Statistics New Zealand is working to improve the timeliness of quarterly Gross Domestic Product statistics, which it concedes are too old by the time they come out, its senior economic statistician said on Monday.
"We would like to see an improvement in the timeliness this year. That would be our goal," Stephen Hickson told Reuters.

"At the moment we're investigating the possibility of bringing forward the release from 13 weeks after the reference quarter, which is what it currently is, to somewhere around about 10 or 11, which is comparable to many other countries."
GDP statistics for the September quarter will be released on Thursday, but economists say the numbers are too historical to be of tangible significance to financial markets by the time they come out.

"It's a complete pain because it's the one that would actually help us the most in knowing exactly what's going on in the economy, and yet we get it so late," said Stuart Marshall, economic analyst at Bancorp Treasury Services.
Hickson said September quarter data could have been released on December 31, but the Christmas holiday period made that impracticable.

"And we would have to improve our timeliness by a week at least to bring it out before Christmas. Originally that's where the timeliness improvement impetus came from, to try and bring out the September quarter earlier," he said.
Many other countries with better timeliness had more monthly data than New Zealand, which tended to have only quarterly information.

"We have to bring forward the collection of those quarterly surveys, such as the manufacturing survey, much of the international trade and finance information on imports and exports and that type of thing," Hickman said.
"It involves the whole survey cycle. We have to get respondents replying earlier, that's essentially the key."
He said SNZ was currently costing out timeliness initiatives, and if additional funding was needed, it would be sought from Treasury.
"If we were going to have to increase our resources to bring forward the quarterly manufacturing survey, then yes, we may have to approach Treasury for extra funding," he said.
Efforts were also being made to improve the timeliness of the release of balance of payments data.

"Part of the reason for that is that the balance of payments feed into the quarterly GDP release on the expenditure side. So improvements in timeliness for the balance of payments will have to occur to bring GDP forward," Hickman said.
